meta.title: PR 512: cursor paging for the task list, explained
meta.summary: The task list used page numbers, so tasks jumped or repeated when a teammate added one mid scroll. This PR pages by a cursor instead. Taskflow and this PR are fictional.

context.problem: Page numbers shift when rows are added. A teammate creating a task while you scroll makes the next page repeat one task, and deleting one makes you skip a task.
goals: No repeated or skipped tasks while scrolling
The same speed on page 50 as on page 1
Old clients keep working for one release
nonGoals: Changing the sort order users see
context.background: Offset paging asks Postgres to count past every earlier row, so deep pages also got slower as teams grew.

nodes.label: Task list page
nodes.summary: Asks for the next page as you reach the bottom.

nodes.label: Tasks API
nodes.summary: Reads the cursor from the query and returns the next one.

nodes.label: Cursor codec

nodes.summary: Finds the next rows with an index on created time and id.

diff.summary: New codec. It base64 encodes the last task's created time and id, and rejects anything it did not make.
listTasks() now takes an after position and asks for rows strictly after it, instead of an offset.
Reads cursor from the query string, returns nextCursor, and still accepts page for one release.
Adds an index on team, created time and id, which the new query walks in order.
Keeps nextCursor from each response and sends it with the next request.
Adds a test that inserts a task between two page loads and checks nothing repeats.

flows.title: Next page, before
flows.trigger: You scroll to the bottom of the list
flows.summary: Page numbers count rows, so new rows shift every later page.

steps.label: GET /api/tasks?page=3
steps.detail: The page asks for rows 41 to 60.

steps.label: Lists with offset 40
steps.detail: The service turns the page number into an offset.

steps.label: Skips 40 rows, takes 20
steps.detail: Postgres walks past 40 rows first. If a task was added at the top, row 41 is a task you already saw.

steps.label: Returns 20 tasks
steps.detail: One of them can be a repeat.

flows.title: Next page, after
flows.trigger: You scroll to the bottom of the list
flows.summary: The cursor names the last task you saw, so new rows cannot shift the next page.

steps.label: GET with the last cursor
steps.detail: The page sends back the nextCursor it got last time.

steps.label: Decodes the cursor
steps.detail: A cursor this server did not make is a 400, not a guess.
steps.why: An opaque cursor lets the format change later without breaking clients that only pass it back.

steps.label: Lists after that task
steps.detail: The service gets a created time and an id, not a number.

steps.label: Seeks past the cursor
steps.detail: WHERE (createdAt, id) < (cursor) uses the new index, so page 50 costs the same as page 1.
steps.why: The id breaks ties between tasks created in the same millisecond; created time alone would skip one.

steps.label: Returns tasks and nextCursor
steps.detail: No repeats, even if a teammate added tasks meanwhile.

risks.risk: Old mobile builds still send page numbers
risks.mitigation: The API keeps accepting page for one release and logs each use.

risks.risk: The new index slows task inserts
risks.mitigation: Measured on a copy of production: inserts went from 2.1 ms to 2.3 ms.

risks.risk: A crafted cursor reads another team's tasks
risks.mitigation: The query always filters by the caller's team, and the codec rejects cursors it did not sign.

rollout.label: Ship the index migration first
rollout.detail: Built concurrently, so writes never block.

rollout.label: Deploy the API with both page and cursor
Switch the web app to cursors
Remove page support after the next mobile release

quiz.question: A teammate deletes a task while you are on page 2. With this PR, what happens when you load page 3?
options: You see the next 20 tasks, none skipped
You get an error because the cursor task is gone
quiz.explain: The cursor holds a position, not a row to look up, so rows after it are found even if that task is gone. Skipping a task was the old offset behavior, which is what this PR removes.

quiz.question: Lists are fast on page 1 but slow on page 50. Which part would you check first?
quiz.explain: Without the index on created time and id, Postgres has to sort before it can seek. The codec only packs two values, so it cannot cause a slowdown that grows with depth.

quiz.question: Why does the cursor include the id and not only the created time?
options: Two tasks can share a created time, so time alone could skip one
The id makes the cursor harder to guess
quiz.explain: Bulk imports create tasks in the same millisecond, and the id breaks the tie. Guessing is stopped by signing and the team filter, not by the id.

glossary.definition: An opaque string that marks where the last page ended.
Asking for rows by number: skip 40, take 20.
A query that starts after a known row, using an index, instead of counting rows.

walkthroughs.title: The cursor codec
walkthroughs.why: Every page after the first trusts this decoder, so it decides what a client may ask for.

steps.note: A position is the last task's created time plus its id.
steps.why: Two tasks can share a created time; the id breaks the tie, so no task is skipped at a page edge.

steps.note: Signs the position and packs it into one URL safe string.
steps.why: Clients treat it as an opaque token, so the format can change later without breaking them.

steps.note: Unpacks a cursor the client sent back and checks it has all three parts.
Refuses any cursor whose signature this server did not make.
steps.why: A hand made cursor could otherwise point anywhere; the team filter in the service is the second guard.

steps.note: Returns the position as a real date and id for the query.

walkthroughs.takeaway: A cursor is a signed bookmark: the server only accepts bookmarks it wrote itself.

walkthroughs.title: The keyset query
walkthroughs.why: This query is why pages no longer repeat or skip tasks, and why page 50 is as fast as page 1.

steps.note: Every query is limited to the caller's team.
steps.why: Even a valid cursor from another team can never widen what this returns.

steps.note: Asks only for tasks strictly after the bookmark: older, or the same time with a smaller id.
steps.why: Rows added above the bookmark cannot shift what comes after it, unlike an offset.

steps.note: Sorts by created time, then id, the same order as the new index.
steps.why: Postgres walks the index in order and stops after the page, instead of counting past earlier rows.

steps.note: Takes one row more than the page.
steps.why: The extra row says whether a next page exists without a separate count.

steps.note: Returns the page and a cursor for its last task, or none at the end.

walkthroughs.takeaway: Paging by position, not by count, is what makes the list stable while it changes.
